If you collect Social Security, several automatic changes are headed your way in just a matter of weeks. The Social Security Administration (SSA) has already locked in next year's numbers, and they touch everything from your monthly check to how much you can earn at a job without losing part of your benefit. Some of these adjustments happen behind the scenes, no action required. Others depend on you reviewing a notice, updating your information, or doing a little math before December 31. Here's what's changing, and what you may want to look at before the calendar flips. Read More Here › SPONSORED Your monthly benefit is getting a cost-of-living boost Social Security beneficiaries will see a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) beginning in January 2027, according to the SSA. The COLA, which adjusts benefits based on inflation measured by the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), applies to nearly 72 million Social Security beneficiaries. SSI recipients will see their increased payments slightly earlier, starting December 31, 2026. On average, retirement benefits will rise by about $75 a month, with the average retired worker's benefit moving from an estimated $2,095 to $2,170 a month after the COLA, per the SSA's 2027 COLA fact sheet. This adjustment happens automatically — you don't need to apply or request it. What to do: Watch for your personalized COLA notice. The SSA says most beneficiaries will be able to view it online in the Message Center of their personal Social Security account starting in late November 2026. If you haven't opted into online messages, a paper notice will arrive by mail in December. Either way, it's worth reading closely, since it shows your exact new benefit amount and any deductions, such as Medicare premiums. Shopping for cheaper auto insurance? Enter your zip code here to get started. The earnings limit is rising for people who work and collect benefits If you're younger than full retirement age (FRA) and still working while collecting Social Security, the SSA limits how much you can earn before it temporarily withholds part of your benefit. That limit is going up in 2027. For people who are under full retirement age for all of 2027, the earnings limit will rise to $25,560 a year (about $2,130 a month), up from $24,480 in 2026, according to the SSA. The SSA withholds $1 in benefits for every $2 earned above that threshold. For those reaching full retirement age sometime in 2027, the limit is higher: $67,920 a year (about $5,660 a month), up from $65,160 in 2026. In that case, the SSA withholds $1 for every $3 earned above the limit, and this rule only applies to earnings in the months before you reach FRA. Once you reach full retirement age, the earnings test disappears entirely. There is no limit on how much you can earn without affecting your benefit. What to do: If you're still working and claiming benefits before FRA, it may help to estimate your 2027 wages now. Higher limits generally mean you can earn more before any withholding kicks in, which could change how you think about part-time work, consulting income, or a planned raise. The SSA's online earnings test calculator can help you see how your specific income may affect your benefit. Full retirement age continues its generational shift Full retirement age, the age at which you qualify for 100% of your calculated benefit, is 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later, per the SSA. This isn't a 2027-specific change, but it's worth keeping in mind as you plan around other adjustments, since your FRA determines which earnings-test threshold applies to you and how much your benefit may be reduced for early claiming or increased for delayed claiming. What to do: If you're unsure of your exact full retirement age, the SSA's retirement age calculator can confirm it based on your birth date. Learn More Here › SPONSORED The maximum taxable earnings amount is increasing Workers who are still paying into Social Security will also see a change. The maximum amount of earnings subject to Social Security tax, known as the taxable maximum, will rise to $192,300 in 2027, up from $184,500 in 2026, according to the SSA. Earnings above that amount aren't subject to the 6.2% Social Security payroll tax, though they also don't count toward future benefit calculations. This adjustment happens automatically through payroll withholding and self-employment tax calculations. There's nothing to update with the SSA directly, but higher earners may want to factor it into year-end tax planning. What to do: If you're self-employed or a higher earner, it may help to revisit your 2027 tax withholding or estimated payments with a tax professional, since the higher taxable maximum could mean a larger Social Security tax bill next year. Disability thresholds are adjusting too For people receiving Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) or considering applying, the substantial gainful activity (SGA) threshold — the amount of monthly earnings generally considered too high to qualify as disabled — is increasing. For 2027, the non-blind SGA amount rises to $1,770 a month, and the blind SGA amount rises to $2,950 a month, according to the SSA. The trial work period threshold, which lets SSDI beneficiaries test working without immediately losing benefits, increases to $1,270 a month. What to do: If you receive SSDI and are weighing a return to work, these higher thresholds generally give you more room to earn before it affects your eligibility determination. The SSA's Ticket to Work program and your local field office can help clarify how work affects your specific case. SSI payment standards are going up Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients will see their federal payment standard rise to $1,029 a month for an individual and $1,544 a month for a couple in 2027, up from $994 and $1,491, respectively, in 2026, per the SSA. As noted above, this increase technically lands in beneficiaries' accounts on December 31, 2026, ahead of the broader January Social Security COLA. What to do: SSI recipients may want to confirm their state supplement amount, if applicable, since some states add their own payment on top of the federal standard and update their own schedules separately. Retirement News: Almost 80% of Americans fear a retirement age increase — here’s the real reason why Bottom line Most of these 2027 changes, including the COLA increase, the higher taxable maximum, and the new earnings-test thresholds, happen automatically. You don't need to file paperwork for the SSA to apply them. But a few minutes reviewing your COLA notice, checking your Social Security account, and running your expected 2027 earnings through the SSA's calculators can help you avoid surprises, especially if you're still working while collecting benefits. With less than 10 weeks until these changes take effect, now is a reasonable time to review your retirement budget , log into your my Social Security account, confirm your mailing and direct deposit information are current, and set a reminder to check your Message Center in late November when notices start appearing online.
